turns.en: I mean, we only have so many different ways to manipulate neurons. But in the health realm, I love that you're bringing this up because it really bridges the two areas that we've been talking about, public health discourse and neuroscience, reading, writing to the nervous system.
turns.zh: 我是说，我们操纵神经元的方式就那么多。但在健康这个领域，我很高兴你提起这个，因为它真正把我们一直在谈的两块——公共健康讨论，以及神经科学里对神经系统的读取和写入——连接了起来。

turns.en: And it bridges the two because what are we talking about? Get morning sunlight. Why? To set your circadian rhythm, spike your cortisol. It seems like a blunt tool, but there's a circuit in place from your eye to your hypothalamus and on and on that is there for that purpose.
turns.zh: 它把两者连起来，因为我们到底在谈什么？晒清晨的阳光。为什么？为了设定你的昼夜节律（circadian rhythm）、让皮质醇（cortisol）上来一下。它看起来是个钝器，但从你的眼睛到下丘脑，再往下、再往下，本来就有一条回路是为这个目的存在的。

turns.en: So it's not biohacking, right? This is important. It's not like using a paperclip to fix my glasses. That's not what the paperclip was designed for.
turns.zh: 所以它不是生物黑客，对吧？这一点很重要。它不像用回形针去修我的眼镜——回形针本来就不是为这个设计的。

turns.en: It's not a good solution. It's a temporary solution. The problem with a lot of pharmacology, like SSRIs, believe it or not, helped so many people with true clinical grade OCD, they were overprescribed for depression.
turns.zh: 那不是个好方案，只是个临时方案。很多药理学的问题在于，比如 SSRIs（选择性血清素再摄取抑制剂），信不信由你，它们帮了非常多真正临床级强迫症（OCD）的人，而它们被过度开给了抑郁症。

turns.en: And really what they do is increase serotonin, which allows for more neuroplasticity. Now everyone's down on SSRIs, understandably so, although they have their place, but everyone's really excited about psilocybin.
turns.zh: 而它们真正做的是增加血清素，从而带来更多神经可塑性。现在大家都在贬低 SSRIs，这可以理解，尽管它们有其一席之地；而大家对裸盖菇素（psilocybin）则非常兴奋。

turns.en: What is psilocybin? It increases serotonin and massively so it unmasks lateral connections in the brain, allows you to form new associations in a very condensed timeframe.
turns.zh: 什么是裸盖菇素？它大幅增加血清素，从而揭开（unmask）大脑里的横向连接，让你在一个非常压缩的时间窗里形成新的联结。

turns.en: Sometimes it works great, sometimes not, but it's interesting. Same thing with MDMA. Create really massive increases in neuromodulators in a specific context that we're going to work on this thing, this pain, this issue, this trauma, this depression, and you get more plasticity than you do if you're just lazing away at the problem through talking about it day in, day out.
turns.zh: 有时候它效果极好，有时候不然，但这很有意思。MDMA 也一样——在一个特定情境里造成神经调质的大幅激增：我们要来处理这件事、这种痛苦、这个问题、这段创伤、这种抑郁，于是你获得的可塑性，远超过你日复一日只是慢吞吞地谈论这个问题所得到的。

turns.en: You need the therapy, but what did you really do to create plasticity? You put serotonin through the roof with psilocybin, or in the case of MDMA, you increase serotonin and dopamine and you have this heightened opportunity for plasticity, okay, TMS.
turns.zh: 你需要治疗，但你到底做了什么来创造可塑性？你用裸盖菇素把血清素冲到天花板；或者在 MDMA 的情形，你增加血清素和多巴胺，于是获得了这个被放大的可塑性机会。好，还有 TMS。

turns.en: Or what I think will soon happen is combine transcradial magnetic stimulation and pharmacology in order to work through a clinical issue. That is of emotions or mind, like depression, like PTSD.
turns.zh: 或者我认为很快会发生的是：把经颅磁刺激（TMS）和药理学结合起来，以处理一个临床问题——情绪或心智上的问题，比如抑郁症、比如 PTSD（创伤后应激障碍）。

turns.en: So these two things are going to start to intersect. ADHD with stimulants, yep, ramps up activity in the prefrontal cortex, and you can focus better on things that you normally wouldn't be able to focus on.
turns.zh: 所以这两样东西会开始交叉。ADHD（注意缺陷多动障碍）用兴奋剂——没错，它会拉高前额叶皮层的活动，于是你能更好地专注在那些平时你根本无法专注的事情上。

turns.en: It's just a non-specific focus enhancer because it increases activity there. You could also do sleep creatine, in particular when sleep deprived.
turns.zh: 它只是一种非特异性的专注增强剂，因为它提升了那里的活动。你还可以借助睡眠和肌酸（creatine），尤其是在睡眠不足的时候。

turns.en: Is it like Adderall? No. But those two things, great night's sleep, plus some caffeine, you're pretty close to Adderall level effects. It's just that the people taking Adderall aren't getting great sleep.
turns.zh: 它像 Adderall 吗？不像。但这两样——一场好觉，加上一些咖啡因——你差不多就能接近 Adderall 水平的效果。只是吃 Adderall 的人往往没有睡好。

turns.en: And so we were really talking about tools of different types, different margins of safety, but they are all very blunt because all these receptors are expressed everywhere.
turns.zh: 所以我们其实是在谈各种类型、不同安全边际的工具，但它们全都非常钝，因为所有这些受体（receptors）都表达在每个地方。

turns.en: So you get sexual side effects, weight gain or excessive weight loss with certain antidepressants or hypersexuality with certain drugs, et cetera, because these receptors are all over the brain.
turns.zh: 所以你会看到：某些抗抑郁药带来性功能方面的副作用、体重增加或过度减重，某些药物带来性欲亢进，等等——因为这些受体遍布整个大脑。

turns.en: The same thing with electrical stimulation, you just want more spatial and temporal specificity. It has to go that way. Neuroscience went that way in terms of reading and understanding the nervous system.
turns.zh: 电刺激也是一样，你就是想要更高的空间和时间特异性，它必须朝那个方向走。神经科学在读取和理解神经系统方面就走过那个方向。

turns.en: You can talk about Dario's work, for instance, no one talks about his work in this realm, but he was recording in Mike Berry's lab from retinas, usually Salamander retina or some other creature, and they record as many neurons as you could.
turns.zh: 你可以拿 Dario 的工作来说，比如——没人谈他在这方面的研究——但他在 Mike Berry 的实验室里从视网膜做记录，通常是蝾螈（salamander）视网膜或别的什么生物，尽可能多地记录神经元。

turns.en: And then you knew what visual signals you were giving the retina, so you knew the input, you knew the responses at the level of photoreceptors, the output cells, what we call ganglion cells, the signals going off to the brain.
turns.zh: 然后你知道你给视网膜的是什么视觉信号，所以你知道输入，你知道光感受器（photoreceptors）层面的反应、知道输出细胞——也就是我们所说的神经节细胞（ganglion cells）——知道传向大脑的信号。

turns.en: And the goal was get as much information about the total collection of neurons responding to an image so we can move from image to perception deep in the brain.
turns.zh: 目标是尽可能多地获取关于「响应一幅图像的所有神经元」这一总集合的信息，好让我们从图像一路走到大脑深处的知觉。

turns.en: Now you're still a few steps away from the actual perception, which takes place in the brain. But those and the guys that they were trained under, Marcus Meister and others, those were heroes of our field because dropping electrodes in an area and buzzing and like the animal goes into a rage or it starts mating or whatever, that's super cool.
turns.zh: 当然，离实际在大脑中发生的知觉你还差几步。但这些人，以及带他们的导师——Marcus Meister 等人——都是我们领域的英雄。因为往某个区域插入电极、通上电，动物就暴怒、或者开始交配，诸如此类——那太酷了。

turns.en: But then you have to move to like, what's the nature of the switch in real life? And people are studying those things. What moves an animal from exploring mating to actual mating?
turns.zh: 但你得进一步问：现实里那个开关的本质是什么？人们在研究这些。是什么让动物从「试探性地求偶」进入「真正交配」？

turns.en: What moves an animal from exploring an aggressive interaction to an actual aggressive interaction? But these are all still very low level behaviors and motivations.
turns.zh: 是什么让动物从「试探性的攻击性互动」变成「真正的攻击性互动」？但这些还都是很低层的行为和动机。

turns.en: And we're just starting to understand those. So the cyborg thing, like, can I increase your creativity? We're not even close to that. We don't even know what circuit.
turns.zh: 我们才刚刚开始理解这些。所以「赛博格」那一套——比如，我能不能提高你的创造力？我们连边都还没摸到，我们甚至不知道是哪条回路。

turns.en: Or IQ or something. Yeah, I mean, you could imagine stimulating more memory capacity, but you might give up something. You want to hear something super creepy?
turns.zh: 或者智力（IQ）之类的。是的，我是说，你能想象刺激出更多的记忆容量，但你可能要牺牲掉别的什么东西。你想听一件特别瘆人的事吗？

turns.en: This might freak out your audience, but it's true. So a few years back, there was a guy, his first name is He. That's how you pronounce it. H-E.
turns.zh: 这可能会让你的听众吓一跳，但这是真的。几年前，有个人，他的名字念作 He——就是这么发的音，H-E。

turns.en: I can't pronounce his last name. He actually had done his postdoctoral training at Stanford, and then he moved on to his own lab in China. He announced to the world at a meeting that he had done CRISPR in twin babies.
turns.zh: 他的姓我发不准。他其实曾在 Stanford 做博士后，然后回到中国建立了自己的实验室。他在一个会议上向全世界宣布，他对一对双胞胎婴儿做了 CRISPR（基因编辑）。

turns.en: He had deleted the HIV receptor. And the story was, and I don't know if it's true or not, but that the father of these children was HIV positive, and he wanted to save these kids from getting HIV AIDS.
turns.zh: 他删除了 HIV 的受体。事情据说是——我不知道真假——孩子的父亲是 HIV 阳性，而他想让这些孩子免于感染 HIV、免于艾滋（AIDS）。

turns.en: There was this moment in the medical science community where no one knew how people would react. Were they going to give them a Nobel Prize or throw them in jail?
turns.zh: 在医学科学界有那么一个时刻，没人知道人们会作何反应。他们是要给他发诺贝尔奖，还是把他关进监狱？

turns.en: He went to the end experiment. We know how to do this now. The technologies exist, but he just did it. And there was this really weird sociology around this in the science community where people who had worked with him prior, who had exchanged emails with him, their emails now were, like, people were digging into the emails, and it was clear that the communications from a lot of these people were sort of the, hey, be careful, but like, is it working?
turns.zh: 他一路做到了底、做成了实验。我们现在知道怎么做了，技术已经存在，但他就这么直接做了。科学界围绕这件事出现了一种很奇怪的社会生态——那些以前跟他共事过、跟他通过邮件的人，现在人们开始翻检他们的邮件，而很清楚的是，很多人的通信无非是：嘿，小心点，但——它真的能成吗？

turns.en: Is it working? But everyone was waiting. Like, if he gets in trouble, I didn't know the guy, right? And I didn't know the guy for the record.
turns.zh: 它真的能成吗？但所有人都在观望：要是他惹上麻烦，我可不认识这家伙，对吧？说句实话，我本来就不认识他。

turns.en: I didn't know the guy. I knew of him because, you know, I knew the lab he worked in, but it's like, am I going to be a part of this? Like, was I important for this important discovery or should I dissociate myself from this?
turns.zh: 我不认识他本人，只是听说过他，因为我知道他待过的那个实验室。但那种感觉是：我要不要成为这件事的一部分？在这个重大发现里我算不算重要？还是我应该跟它撇清关系？

turns.en: And it turns out the world decided, like, no, ethically, this is bad. The Chinese government came out and said that his lab would be taken away and he'll be punished in some way.
turns.zh: 结果这个世界做出的裁定是：不，从伦理上这是错的。中国政府出面说，要撤掉他的实验室，他会被以某种方式惩处。

turns.en: I don't know how he was going to be punished. You know what? Disappeared. Yeah. Do you know what that guy's doing right now? He has a laboratory purportedly in Austin, Texas.
turns.zh: 我不知道他会被怎么惩处。你猜怎么着——他消失了。是啊。你知道这家伙现在在干什么吗？据说他在德州奥斯汀有个实验室。

turns.en: Okay. Now, I don't know if that's true or not. So my first reaction is like, how did that happen? My second reaction is, wait, of course, he wasn't the only person doing this.
turns.zh: 好。我不知道这到底是不是真的。所以我第一反应是：那怎么会发生？第二反应是：等等，当然了，他不是唯一一个在做这种事的人。

turns.en: Like, you know, this is happening in labs all over the world is just no one's talking about it because he proved that it's dangerous to talk about.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，这种事正在全世界的实验室里发生，只是没人说——因为他证明了「说出来」是危险的。

turns.en: Now, I think it's very important to have the ethics and the committee set up for this kind of technology. But then you take a step back and say, like, where are we in the world of genetic engineering humans?
turns.zh: 我认为，为这类技术设立伦理和委员会非常重要。但退一步看，你会问：在「对人类做基因工程」这件事上，我们到底走到哪了？

turns.en: And you say, okay, well, they do testing of amniotic fluid in pregnant women babies. Commonplace people can refuse it, I believe, but in general, that's done.
turns.zh: 然后你说：好吧，孕妇会做羊水检测，检查胎儿。这很常见，人们可以拒绝，我相信，但一般而言，这都在做。

turns.en: People are screening embryos for IVF, they're companies like Herosite and Orchid. Some are more focused on trying to see if there are any diseases.
turns.zh: 人们在为 IVF（试管婴儿）筛选胚胎，有像 Herosite 和 Orchid 这样的公司。有些更专注于看看有没有任何疾病。

turns.en: Some are trying to link certain genetic patterns of expression to autism, but also to IQ, to height, et cetera. So you can see where this is going.
turns.zh: 有些则试图把某些基因表达模式与自闭症联系起来，也与智力（IQ）、身高等等联系起来。所以你能看出这会走向哪里。

turns.en: And then of course, there's this thing that we call partner selection. People choose, in most cases, not always, but they choose who to get sperm from or eggs from in the context of relationship, right?
turns.zh: 然后当然，还有我们所说的「伴侣选择」。大多数情况下——虽非总是——人们会挑选，在一段关系里，用谁的精子、谁的卵子，对吧？

turns.en: Or if people are using a sperm donor, they're choosing on the basis of like you look at the criteria and the criteria like height, where they go to school, what do they look like?
turns.zh: 或者如果人们用的是精子捐赠者，他们是照着标准选的——你看那些标准：身高、上哪所学校、长什么样。

turns.en: So the lines between these haven't been cleanly defined, but you can see there's a gradation there. Now, I don't know if he's actually in Austin, Texas, or if he's actually doing these experiments.
turns.zh: 所以这些之间的界限并没有被清晰地划出来，但你能看到那里有一条渐变。话说回来，我不知道他是不是真在德州奥斯汀，也不知道他是不是真在做这些实验。

turns.en: I don't know that. I want to be very clear, but I find it fascinating and important to understand that people are going to run with these technologies.
turns.zh: 我不知道。我想说清楚这一点。但我觉得，认识到人们会拿着这些技术一路狂奔，这既迷人又重要。

turns.en: How fast they run, where they get implemented isn't clear. What about memory? The HIV receptor supposedly is also linked to some aspects of neural circuit formation that are linked to memory.
turns.zh: 他们跑得多快、会在哪里落地，并不清楚。那记忆呢？据说 HIV 那个受体也与神经回路形成的某些方面相关，而这些又与记忆相关。

turns.en: So there was this other layer of those experiments that everyone knew in the neuroscience community but wasn't talking about, which was, was he actually trying to both render those kids immune from HIV infection, but also make them super smart?
turns.zh: 所以那些实验还有一层，神经科学界人人都知道却没人说：他是不是既想让这些孩子对 HIV 感染免疫，又想让他们变得超级聪明？

turns.en: And no one's been able to answer that question conclusively, but there is this idea that maybe people are genetically engineering people that have some gene expression or lack of gene expression, which renders them more cognitively or physically capable.
turns.zh: 没人能对这个问题给出定论，但有这样一种想法：也许人们正在通过基因工程制造某些带有或缺乏某种基因表达的人，从而让他们在认知上或体能上更强。

turns.en: And you go, oh, that sounds crazy. Yeah. And the full of statin gene has been mutated in animals and there are people doing gene therapy for full of statin to try and build more muscle.
turns.zh: 你会说，哦，那听起来很疯狂。是啊。肌肉生长抑制素（myostatin）基因已经在动物身上被突变过，也有人正在做针对 myostatin 的基因治疗，试图长出更多肌肉。

turns.en: So if this was 15 years ago and you and I were having this conversation, you'd be like, guys, that was mine. Guys, that was mine. Everything I just described has happened.
turns.zh: 所以如果这是十五年前你我这样一场对话，你会说：老兄，那是科幻；老兄，太扯了。可我刚描述的每一件事都已经发生了。

turns.en: Why it happened exactly what they were trying to do unclear, whether or not it's still ongoing, whether or not this guy's actually in Austin, Texas, doing these experiments where he's someplace else or he's sitting in a prison someplace in China.
turns.zh: 至于到底为什么发生、他们究竟想做什么，还不清楚；它是否仍在进行也不清楚；这人到底是不是在奥斯汀做这些实验、还是在别处、还是正坐在中国某地的监狱里，都不清楚。

turns.en: I don't know. Okay. I think it'll be interesting. The internet will tell us. Yeah. I guess I'm more excited than concerned, provided people are talking about it and people are thinking about it really carefully.
turns.zh: 我不知道。好吧，我觉得这会很有意思，互联网会告诉我们答案。是啊，我想我是兴奋多于担忧——只要人们在谈论它、在认真思考它。

turns.en: One of the beautiful things about social media is nothing stays a secret for very long. If at all, nothing stays a secret. There are no secrets anymore.
turns.zh: 社交媒体美好的一点在于，没有什么秘密能藏太久——或者说压根什么秘密都藏不住，这世上再也没有秘密了。

turns.en: You can have a vaulted conversation with somebody. That absolutely is true. But as soon as more than two people know about something, you can't exist in this world without leaving a digital footprint.
turns.zh: 你可以跟某人有私密谈话，那当然属实。但只要一件事被超过两个人知道，你只要活在这个世界上，就难免留下数字足迹。

turns.en: So sooner or later, we'll hear. It seems like the arc of all this is just control. Like control of genetics, control of brain states, control of all these things through technology over time.
turns.zh: 所以迟早我们会听到风声。这一切的走向，似乎就是「控制」——随着时间推移，通过技术去控制基因、控制大脑状态、控制所有这些。

turns.en: And this is very much like a William Gibson future is here just not evenly distributed yet. All the future is here type things. What excites you most of all this stuff?
turns.zh: 这非常像 William Gibson 那句「未来已来，只是分布还不均匀」。诸如此类「未来都已在这里」的话。这一切里，最让你兴奋的是什么？

turns.en: If you had to pinpoint, like if I forced you to go start a company or something and just focus on one thing. I spent a lot of time thinking about media and culture and just humans generally.
turns.zh: 如果要一锤定音的话，比如我逼你去创办一家公司、只专注做一件事。我花了大量时间思考媒体、文化，以及笼统地说——人。

turns.en: So to me, the most exciting thing is that because of social media, we're all in the same campus. X is that campus, Instagram to some degree, but those are the campuses for the communication about these things.
turns.zh: 所以对我来说，最令人兴奋的是：因为有了社交媒体，我们都在同一个校园里。X 就是那个校园，Instagram 在某种程度上也是——它们是围绕这些事情交流的校园。

turns.en: What I'm excited about is the idea that we've got so many more people learning about things in their field and adjacent to their field that there are a bunch of things that we can't predict that are going to happen.
turns.zh: 让我兴奋的是这个念头：现在有远为更多的人在学自己领域内、以及领域相邻的东西，于是会有很多我们预测不到的事情发生。

turns.en: Like someone in the human gene therapy space who's an amazing educator has the charisma and the ability to talk about these things, but also has the chops really understands it is going to move that space forward at tremendous velocity at some point.
turns.zh: 比如，在人类基因治疗领域，有一位出色的教育者，他有人格魅力、有能力谈论这些东西，同时又有真功夫、真正理解它——到了某个时刻，他会以极高的速度推动这个领域向前。

turns.en: The issue is that it was a scientist just like doing his thing and he just kind of went a rogue and did it. He didn't check with anybody. When I was coming up, you did experiments at night and the goal was like, don't kill yourself.
turns.zh: 问题在于，那只是一个科学家在做自己的事，然后他有点走偏、径自把它做了。他没跟任何人商量。在我成长的年代，你会在晚上做实验，目标是：别把自己弄死。

turns.en: Don't burn down the lab. Don't break protocol, but like do experiments. Now it's changed a little bit. Everyone's a little bit more paranoid.
turns.zh: 别把实验室烧了，别违规，但要做实验。如今情况有点变了，每个人都更多疑了一些。

turns.en: I'm excited that somebody and they're starting. I think that people are thinking about neuro technologies to read and write from the nervous system in awake states.
turns.zh: 我兴奋的是，已经有人——而且他们在起步。我觉得人们正在思考用于在清醒状态下读取和写入神经系统的神经技术。

turns.en: My own interest right now is really understanding the waking states. We understand slow wave sleep, deep sleep and one and two and three sleep wrote a whole chapter in the book about sleep, its architecture, how temperature changes one or the other heat up the bed in the morning or the room in the morning, you get more REM.
turns.zh: 我自己现在的兴趣，是真正去理解清醒状态。我们理解慢波睡眠、深睡眠，以及一二三期睡眠——我在书里为睡眠写了整整一章，讲它的架构、讲温度如何变化、如何在早上把床或房间升温，从而让你获得更多 REM。

turns.en: We know all that stuff. We know so much about sleep and how to measure and now nudge and maybe even dial in sleep really precisely with these I'm asked type tools, changing the room temp is pretty crude compared to that, but it's also helpful.
turns.zh: 我们懂这些。关于睡眠我们了解得非常多——如何测量、如今如何微调，甚至用这些 Eight Sleep 之类的工具把睡眠精确地「调准」；相比之下，改房间温度相当粗糙，但也很有用。

turns.en: I want to understand waking brain states. I don't know how to describe the state that we're in REM is not language about how you feel in REM.
turns.zh: 我想理解清醒状态下的大脑状态。我不知道该如何描述我们此刻所处的状态——REM 并不是用来描述「你在 REM 里有什么感觉」的语言。

turns.en: It's rapid eye movements. There's something associated with the state that we're in right now. Like I'm alert. I'm focused. I'm enjoying our discussion.
turns.zh: 它只是快速眼动而已。而与我们此刻所处的状态相关的，是某种东西——比如我很清醒、很专注、我很享受我们的讨论。

turns.en: What is this state? We need much better understanding of waking states and which waking states lend themselves better to which activities. Then we can start writing to the nervous system to generate those states with a lot of temporal and spatial precision.
turns.zh: 这到底是什么状态？我们需要对清醒状态、以及哪些清醒状态更适合哪些活动，有更深的理解。那样我们就能开始写入神经系统，以极高的时间和空间精度去制造那些状态。

turns.en: That to me seems like the most important thing to resolve right now and it's totally doable. I'm not the person to do it because I'm no longer running a lab.
turns.zh: 在我看来，这是当下最该解决的事，而且完全做得到。我不是做这件事的人，因为我不再带实验室了。

turns.en: The problem with neuroscience as a field is a little bit of problem with academia, but even the biotech sector related to neuroscience is that people tend to work on things that are like four degrees off from what their training was.
turns.zh: 神经科学这个领域的问题，某种程度上也是学术界的问题——乃至与神经科学相关的生物科技板块的问题是：人们倾向于做跟自己受训方向相差四度左右的事。

turns.en: Actually, even though I've never met him, I think Dario, even though I disagree with a lot of things I hear from him about AI, I think that it's interesting.
turns.zh: 其实，尽管我从未见过 Dario，尽管我不同意我从他那里听到的关于 AI 的很多东西，我觉得他很有意思。

turns.en: Something came up through neurosciences in this quite different but related field. Sam I've spoken to is extremely smart about the neuroscience, extremely smart as is Zuck, as is Andreessen and Elon obviously understands what he's trying to achieve with Neuralink and he's extremely savvy with respect to like what can be done now, where we need to go.
turns.zh: 有些东西是从神经科学延伸进这个相当不同却相关的领域。我跟 Sam 聊过，他对神经科学极其敏锐、极其聪明——Zuck 也是，Andreessen 也是；而 Elon 显然明白他想用 Neuralink 达成什么，他在「现在能做到什么、我们需要往哪走」上极其精明。

turns.en: In a lot of ways, the technologists who used to just engineer stuff, they're becoming neuroscientists and I love that because neuroscience has always benefited from bringing people in from other fields.
turns.zh: 在很多方面，那些过去只做工程的技术人员，正在变成神经科学家，我很乐见其成——因为神经科学历来受益于从别的领域引进人才。

turns.en: You can't give them the whole problem entirely because as soon as they sink their hands into a brain, they realize this is not a computer. It's something a whole lot more complicated, but bioengineers are getting very, very good.
turns.zh: 你不能把整个问题全交给他们，因为一旦他们把手伸进一个大脑，就明白这不是电脑——它要复杂得多。但生物工程师正变得非常出色。

turns.en: People like Eddie Chang, obviously Neuralink's doing this, Matt McDougal and the folks there and Sam Zuck and Dario, that's a pretty killer lineup and Elon, those four, those are the big four.
turns.zh: 像 Eddie Chang 这样的人——Neuralink 显然也在做——Matt McDougal 和那里的一帮人，还有 Sam Altman、Zuck、Dario——那是一份相当强悍的阵容；还有 Elon。这四个人，是那「四大」。

turns.en: Those are the athletes of brain exploration now. I think most people don't realize that and I'm not sitting here like where the kids say, I'm not trying to like glaze, I think it's just awesome.
turns.zh: 他们就是当下探索大脑的运动员。我想大多数人还没意识到这点。我不是在这儿——用年轻人的话说——想拍谁的马屁（glaze），我只是觉得这太了不起了。

turns.en: You want people coming in who have outside expertise and can leverage the best minds like the best neuroscientists and engineers. So I'm all excitement about it, frankly, but I think we need better definition of waking brain states.
turns.zh: 你需要那些带着外部专长进来、能撬动最顶尖头脑——最顶尖的神经科学家和工程师——的人。所以坦白讲，我对此兴奋不已，但我觉得我们需要把清醒状态下的大脑状态定义得更清楚。

turns.en: I think that's the biggie and the reason I mentioned those different silos that I've touched into is that anytime you see a field, whether or not it's action sports or it's science or it's medicine, take a big leap forward.
turns.zh: 我认为那才是最大的问题。我之所以提到我触及的那些不同领域，是因为无论你看到的是极限运动、科学还是医学，每当一个领域要迈出一大步时——

turns.en: There's always this thing that we talked about earlier where people get into it, some people go public facing, they kind of push the margins a little bit, then it gets too crowded.
turns.zh: 总会出现我们之前谈过的那种情形：人们涌进来，有些人站到台前，把边界往外推一点点，然后那里变得太拥挤。

turns.en: People start getting wacky to get more signal to noise on them. And then the thing kind of dies down. And then there's this surge of really accessible, useful technologies and information.
turns.zh: 人们开始变得古怪，好让自己更出挑、提高信噪比。然后这股热潮多少会退下去。接着一波真正易用、有用的技术和信息就会涌来。

turns.en: So I think 2027, 28 are going to be a low level noise in my estimation around the health space. I mean, that's what the book protocols was about.
turns.zh: 所以在我看来，2027、28 年，围绕健康领域会是一段低噪音期。我是说，我那本《Protocols》讲的就是这些。

turns.en: That's my thesis. We got it. I'm not going to keep talking about morning light. But God's sake, I'm starting to tire myself out. So the reason I can move on from it is because I know it for certain.
turns.zh: 那是我的论点。说完了，我不会再老讲晨光了——天哪，我都快把自己讲腻了。我能从它上面往前走的原因，是我对此确信无疑。

turns.en: What's in the book are the things I know for certain. So now that my thesis is turned in and people can do with it what they will, I think it has things of value, certainly information, but hopefully things of value to people.
turns.zh: 书里写的都是我所确信的东西。现在我的「论文」已经交上去了，大家爱怎么用它就怎么用它。我觉得它里面有价值的东西——肯定有信息，也希望有真正对人有益的东西。

turns.en: Now it's time to move into some other realm. And you can probably tell from today's conversation, I didn't realize this was going to come up.
turns.zh: 现在是时候转向别的领域了。你大概从今天的对话也能看出来——我都没料到这些会被牵扯出来。

turns.en: I am very, very interested in reading and writing from the awake nervous system. Eddie Chang and I talk three times a week for hours at a time.
turns.zh: 我对清醒状态下神经系统的读取和写入，非常、非常感兴趣。Eddie Chang 和我一周聊三次，一聊就是好几个小时。

turns.en: We take walks. Where is neuroscience? What's next? I'm just super excited. It's going to be great. I promise you there's safeguards we need in place, but like the best people are on these problems.
turns.zh: 我们散步。神经科学走到哪了？下一步是什么？我就是超级兴奋，这会非常棒。我向你保证，我们是需要设好安全措施的——但最优秀的一批人正在攻克这些问题。

turns.en: The best people. And that's why it pisses me off when the traditional media tries to slow these people down like, okay, everybody, make your public statement about how you're not going to blow up the world.
turns.zh: 最优秀的一批人。所以每当传统媒体想把这些人拖慢，说「好，每个人都出来做个公开声明，说你不会炸掉世界」，我就来气。

turns.en: It's like, of course. Like you want them to do that. Also, by the way, it doesn't pacify anybody. Of course we need the ethics. We need the safeguards in place, but I'm nothing but excitement about this.
turns.zh: 这就好像——当然了，你也希望他们这么做。顺带一提，这其实安抚不了任何人。我们当然需要伦理、需要设好安全措施，但我对此只有兴奋。

turns.en: And then again, I'm born and raised in Palo Alto. I did not exactly expect our discussion to focus so much on neurotech and waking brain states and things like this, but I honestly hope you and I can do this once a year to check in on the state of this stuff.
turns.zh: 再说了，我在 Palo Alto 出生长大。我没料到我们的讨论会这么聚焦在神经技术、清醒大脑状态这些事上，但我真心希望你我每年能做一次这样的对话，来盘点一下这件事的进展。

turns.en: It does seem like if you really think ahead from the current stuff in AI to where this is all going, of course, inevitably, the intimacy of technology into us is going to increase.
turns.zh: 如果你真从现在 AI 的东西往前推演、想到这一切要走向何方，那确实——技术嵌入我们身内的亲密度，必然会不断提高。

turns.en: And this is like the final frontier. So incredibly fun to talk to you about. When I do this, and I hope it's the first of many, I ask the same traditional closing question.
turns.zh: 而这就像是最后的疆域（final frontier）。跟你聊这个太有意思了。我做这期节目——我希望是许多期里的第一期——都会问同一个传统的收尾问题。

turns.en: What is the kindest thing that someone's done for you? The kindest thing. All right, this is a bit of a weird one, but I've carried the message that I got forward through basically everything.
turns.zh: 有人为你做过的最善良的事是什么？最善良的事。好，这个问题有点怪，但基本上我一直带着我所得到的那句嘱托走过一切。

turns.en: Once people hear it, if they thread it back through portions of today's conversation, I think they'll know how I've done that. So when I was in graduate school, I initially joined a different laboratory.
turns.zh: 等人们听到它、再把它串回今天对话里的某些片段，我想他们就会明白我是怎么做到的。当年读研时，我最初加入的是另一个实验室。

turns.en: You do rotations and I joined a laboratory doing excellent work that was very popular at the time, that was really on the cutting edge of molecular genetic techniques for looking at neurons.
turns.zh: 研究生要做轮转（rotations），而我加入了一个实验室，它做着当时非常热门的出色工作，正处在用分子遗传技术观察神经元的最前沿。

turns.en: And it was all the rage at the time. But I had this absolute love obsession for the work that I had done in my second rotation on stuff and in a field that was pretty crowded.
turns.zh: 那在当时风靡一时。但我对我在第二次轮转里做的东西、对那个相当拥挤的领域里的工作，有一种近乎痴迷的热爱。

turns.en: And I found myself having joined this other lab and sneaking into the lab that interested me more at night and doing experiments. And the woman who ran that lab, which is my graduate advisor, Barbara Chapman, she came to me one day and she just said, listen, I'm totally okay with the fact that you didn't join my lab.
turns.zh: 我发现自己虽然进了那个别的实验室，却会在夜里偷偷溜进那个更让我感兴趣的实验室做实验。而掌管那间实验室、也就是我研究生导师的那位女士 Barbara Chapman，有一天来找我，直接说：听着，你没进我的实验室，我完全没问题。

turns.en: Her lab was already very successful. Anyway, publishing papers and science, et cetera. And she said, but you just seem to really love this stuff.
turns.zh: 她的实验室本来就已经很成功，论文、科研等等都很多。她说：可你看起来是真的热爱这个东西。

turns.en: And the only thing that's really going to determine your success is how badly do you want to know the answers to the questions that you're working on?
turns.zh: 而真正决定你能否成功的唯一东西，是你有多渴望知道你所研究的那些问题的答案。

turns.en: I was like, okay, so I broke up with the other lab. I joined her lab. We published eight first author papers. My career went, but that was all the consequence of working on things to try and answer questions that I was most curious about.
turns.zh: 我当时就：好，于是我离开了那个别的实验室，加入了她的实验室。我们发表了八篇我作为第一作者的论文。我的事业起来了——而这一切，都是去做那些最让我好奇的问题所带来的结果。

turns.en: That was an incredibly kind thing to do. It also required a lot of humility and boldness on her part because she was basically saying like dump them, come back to me.
turns.zh: 那是极其善良的一件事。她那边也需要极大的谦逊和勇气，因为她基本上是在说：甩掉他们，回到我这儿来。

turns.en: And I had to trust that it wasn't because of some sense of rejection in her and it wasn't. She had extremely strong ego. Honestly, I think that's the kindest thing anyone's ever done for me because it showed a belief in me.
turns.zh: 我得相信那不是出于她某种被拒绝的感觉，而确实不是。她其实有非常强大的自我（ego）。说实话，我觉得这是任何人对我做过的最善良的事，因为它表明了她对我的信任。

turns.en: It showed that she understood that I didn't have enough self understanding and enough, frankly, enough guts to just say, I don't want to do the thing that everyone else is super excited about.
turns.zh: 这表明她理解：那时我还没有足够的自我认知，坦白说，也没有足够的胆量去说出——我不想做别人都为之狂热的那件事。

turns.en: I want to focus on the thing that I'm most excited about, which takes a strong mind and is much easier to do once you've had some significant success in a field.
turns.zh: 我想专注于让我最兴奋的那件事——这需要一颗强大的心智，而一旦你在某个领域取得过一些重大成功，做起来就容易得多。

turns.en: It's easy to do when you're like, oh, yeah, everyone said that that was done. That area was done. No one listens to that music, but then we had like two platinum albums.
turns.zh: 当你处在我已经成功的状态时，这样做很容易——大家都说那个已经过时了、那个领域已经做完了，没人再听那种音乐了，可我们却出了两张白金唱片。

turns.en: It's easy to just carry on. But when you're making the decision to go into this area that you know, most people like, why would you go there?
turns.zh: 继续走下去很容易。但当你要做那个决定、走进一个大多数人都说「你为什么要去那儿」的领域时——

turns.en: Like no one works on that anymore. And it turns out that the wheel of the field rotated to and I found myself exiting my PhD lab with the skills that were best suited to what was most important in the field next.
turns.zh: 就好像再没人在做那个了。可结果，这个领域的轮盘转了回来，我发现自己离开博士实验室时掌握的技能，恰恰最适合接下来这个领域最重要的方向。

turns.en: And I had to be very careful because now the landscape matched my internal curiosity. And now I had to make sure, yes, I'm going into this for the right reasons.
turns.zh: 我得非常小心，因为如今外部环境正好与我的内在好奇吻合了，我得确认：我进入这件事，理由是正当的。

turns.en: And it was true. And likewise, I was starting a podcast. I loved running a lab. I truly did love teaching at Stanford. I still do, but it was really, I just have this itch.
turns.zh: 而事实也确实如此。同样地，当我开始做一个播客时——我很热爱带实验室，我真心热爱在 Stanford 教书，至今依然——但真的，我心里就是有那种痒。

turns.en: I've got this knowledge in me that I know people can benefit from. I did not anticipate what came with being public facing. That was like not anticipated.
turns.zh: 我肚子里有这些我知道别人能从中受益的知识。我没预料到站到台前会随之而来什么——那是完全没预料到的。

turns.en: I had no training in that and being media and like, fuck it. I want to do this. And then I just pulled all the stops out and just went for it.
turns.zh: 我在这方面没有任何训练，面对媒体就是：管他呢，我要做这个。然后我就把所有机关全部拉满，径直冲了上去。

turns.en: Here we are. Can you see that line one more time? What was her phrasing of it? Success is determined by how precisely you match your genuine curiosity to the work that you do.
turns.zh: 于是就有了今天的我们。你能再把那句话看一遍吗？她当初是怎么说的？——「你的成功，取决于你在多大程度上把真实的求知欲与你所做的事精准匹配起来。」

turns.en: You do have to understand the field you're in and pay attention to it because all experiments are so hard. Building any company is hard. Doing any podcast, if it's done right, is hard.
turns.zh: 你确实得理解你所在的领域、并关注它，因为所有实验都很难，打造任何公司都很难，把任何播客真正做好也都很难。

turns.en: So you have to make sure that it's really true to you and not to puff him up too much. But I think one of the reasons why Elon is admired by so many people.
turns.zh: 所以你务必要确保那对你来说是真实的。我也不想把他捧得太高，但我觉得，Elon 之所以被那么多人钦佩，原因之一——

turns.en: Yeah, some people dislike him, but I think one of the reasons why deep down people either greatly admire him or envy him is not his money. It's his ability to ignore what people say about what he should be doing.
turns.zh: 是啊，有些人不喜欢他，但我觉得，人们骨子里要么极钦佩他、要么极嫉妒他，原因不是他的钱，而是他能无视别人对他的「应该做什么」指手画脚。

turns.en: I had a guy come on my podcast who I actually like and respect. And he was telling me all the things that Elon and the top technologists should be doing.
turns.zh: 我请过一位我确实喜欢也尊重的人上我的播客，他在那儿告诉我 Elon 和顶尖技术人员应该做的这一堆那一堆事。

turns.en: They should be helping people this way and that way. And I'm like, wait, electric cars and I do think open AI is heading to some very interesting things that relate to medicine and benevolence there and on and on.
turns.zh: 说他们该这样那样地帮助人。我当时就想：等等——还有电动汽车；而我确实认为 OpenAI 正走向一些与医学、与善意相关的非常有趣的方向，如此等等。

turns.en: And he's like, yeah, that's what they should be doing. Not this other stuff, not Mars. That's like telling Metallica to play the Grateful Dead.
turns.zh: 而他说：对，他们就该做这些，别做别的，别去碰火星。这就像叫 Metallica 去弹 Grateful Dead 的歌。

turns.en: Metallica are Metallica because that's what they love. That's the music they fucking love. And the Grateful Dead are the Grateful Dead because that's the music they love.
turns.zh: Metallica 之所以是 Metallica，是因为那是他们热爱的——是他们他妈热爱的音乐；Grateful Dead 之所以是 Grateful Dead，也因为那是他们热爱的音乐。

turns.en: Like you have to be yourself. The big tragedy is when people don't go in the direction of their genuine curiosity because they're trying to quote, unquote, succeed.
turns.zh: 你就是得做自己。最大的悲剧，是人们没有朝自己真实的求知欲走去，因为他们想所谓的——带引号的「成功」。

turns.en: So the kind of thing someone did for me was to gently but very clearly tell me, follow your curiosity, answer the question, solve the problems related to that.
turns.zh: 所以有人为我做的那件善事，就是温柔而非常清楚地告诉我：追随你的好奇心，回答那个问题，去解决与它相关的问题。

turns.en: And you can't go wrong. And to not do that is kind of a slow death. A wonderful, awesome place to close. Andrew, thank you so much for your time.
turns.zh: 你不会走错的；而不这么做，差不多就是一种缓慢的死亡。这是一个绝佳、精彩的收尾。Andrew，非常感谢你抽出时间。
